text: Every person who logs into ServiceNow — agents, managers, end users submitting their own tickets, even integration accounts — is a record on one single table: sys_user. There's no separate employee table and login table hiding somewhere else. It's one table, and nearly everything else in the system, every report, every notification, every script, ultimately points back to a row here.

You create a new user from User Administration, Users, then the New button. The form has dozens of fields, but only a handful matter on day one. User_name is the login value the person actually types — independent of their real name. Email matters for notifications and password resets. And first and last name show up everywhere, from list views to the Impersonate menu to approval records.

Three fields do the real access-control work, and they each answer a different question. Active is the master login gate — set it false and the user cannot log in, no matter what roles or group memberships they hold. Locked_out is a separate flag, usually set automatically after too many failed login attempts, or manually for a security concern. And password_needs_reset forces a fresh password on the very next successful login.

Never delete a departing user's record, even though it's tempting to clean things up. Sys_user is referenced everywhere — an incident's caller_id, an incident's opened_by, a change request's assigned_to, approval history, audit trails on nearly every table. Delete the record and those references break or quietly orphan. Deactivating instead sets active to false and preserves every one of those historical references intact.

A brand-new user record with zero roles can barely do anything beyond viewing their own profile and whatever default guest-level access exposes. Active controls whether they can log in at all. Deactivation preserves history when someone leaves. And real functional access still needs a role assigned — which is exactly where Lesson 2 and Lesson 3 pick up, starting with groups.

Sys_user is the foundation this entire chapter builds on — every group, every role, every ACL you'll meet later all check back against this one table. Next up: groups and group membership, and how ServiceNow actually routes work to a team, not just to one individual person.
